speaker: Amina
text: Everyone sees the AI headlines. But behind every chatbot is a much bigger business story: chips, buildings, electricity—and the race to turn spending into profit. Welcome to Stocks. This is Behind the Move.

speaker: Dexter
text: And the key question is who actually gets paid. A company building AI infrastructure is somebody else's customer. But collecting revenue and earning a lasting return are two different things.

speaker: Amina
text: So let's follow the money. Start with the companies buying computing capacity.

speaker: Dexter
text: Their spending reaches chip and networking suppliers, construction firms, and the businesses running data centers. Cloud providers then sell access to that computing power. Each link has different costs, customers and risks.

speaker: Amina
text: And the physical infrastructure matters just as much as the software. Our AI infrastructure correspondent has been reviewing the energy picture. What stands out?

speaker: Correspondent
text: The scale of the power requirement. The International Energy Agency projects global data-center electricity consumption rising from about four hundred eighty-five terawatt-hours in twenty twenty-five to nine hundred fifty in twenty thirty. That's a projection for all data centers, not AI alone.

speaker: Dexter
text: Does that mean every electricity supplier benefits?

speaker: Correspondent
text: No. Location, grid access and equipment availability matter. The IEA identifies constraints across electricity connections and supply chains. A project announcement doesn't tell us when a facility will actually be operating.

speaker: Amina
text: So there is a difference between announcing investment and delivering capacity.

speaker: Dexter
text: Exactly. And capacity still needs paying customers. Microsoft's latest fiscal fourth-quarter call illustrates the tension: it reported strong cloud demand, while saying infrastructure investment and other factors weighed on its cloud gross-margin percentage.

speaker: Amina
text: Strong demand, but a real cost to serve it.

speaker: Dexter
text: That's why we'll track three things: spending commitments, capacity actually delivered, and whether revenue turns into cash. More investment alone doesn't answer that last question.

speaker: Amina
text: The AI story reaches far beyond one chipmaker. The next chapter is about execution—and returns. That's Behind the Move, on Stocks.
